sections.html:
Three numbers multiply to make your bill: the property's true value, an assessment ratio fixed by the state constitution, and the millage rate where the property sits. Everything gets sorted into one of five classes, and the class picks the ratio.

  • Class I covers a single-family home its owner lives in. Ratio: 10%.
  • Class II is every other kind of real estate not in Class I or IV. Ratio: 15%.
  • Class III is personal property, except vehicles and anything in Class IV. Ratio: 15%.
  • Class IV is public utility property. Ratio: 30%.
  • Class V is cars and trucks. Ratio: 30%.

One mill equals a thousandth of a dollar. The house you live in sits in Class I. Vacant land or a rental falls into Class II and gets the heavier 15% ratio. If you inherited a parent's house and nobody lives in it now, ask the Tax Assessor which class it will land in.

Local elected officials carry most of the load, and the state looks over their shoulder. The Tax Assessor sets value. The Tax Collector takes payment. The Chancery Clerk holds land records and runs the tax sale. The Board of Supervisors hears objections and adopts the rolls.

  • Millage rates come from county boards of supervisors, municipal boards and some school boards.
  • Each parcel owes a county rate and a school district rate, plus a city or levee district rate when it lies inside one.
  • A county has five supervisors, one from each of five districts.
  • The Department of Revenue audits appraisal work, and the State Auditor oversees collection.

Because rates stack by location, a house in town and an equally valued house outside it will not be billed the same.

Whoever holds title on January 1 gets the assessment. Statements show up in November or December, and the deadline to pay is February 1 of the next year. A deadline falling on a weekend or holiday moves to the following Monday with no penalty.

Property tax calendar
StepTiming
Assessment date, owner of recordJanuary 1
Homestead exemption filing windowJanuary 1 to April 1
Ownership instrument filed with Chancery Clerk (for exemption)Before January 7
Assessment appeal to Board of SupervisorsNormally by the first Monday in August
Bills issuedNovember to December
Taxes dueFebruary 1 of the next year
County tax saleFirst Monday in April or last Monday in August, depending on county

Land and buildings are reappraised at least once in four years. Taxable personal property is reappraised annually. An assessor is not required to enter your house, though a walk around the grounds is allowed and a barn that has seen better days still counts.

If the house is your primary residence, you can claim homestead exemption by visiting the county Tax Assessor any time from January 1 to April 1. Approval rolls forward each year until your circumstances change.

  • Tier 1 gives a credit of up to $300 to applicants under 65 who miss the disability tier.
  • Tier 2 serves owners who are 65 or older, or totally disabled, by January 1. It wipes out tax on the first $7,500 of assessed value, which the state also words as the first $75,000 of true value.
  • Tier 3 fully exempts service-connected totally disabled former service members, honorably discharged ones age 90 or more, and certain unremarried spouses of those who died on active duty.

The home must be owned and lived in on January 1, and title must pre-date that day. A deed change, divorce, death, or shift in use or occupancy can trigger a new application. Late income tax filings or vehicle registration problems can get the exemption disallowed, and then you may owe back what was wrongly excused.

Sellers should note that the January 1 owner is who got assessed. If you close after that date but before the bill is settled, make sure the closing statement allocates the tax.

Disagree with the value on your notice? Ask for a hearing in front of the county Board of Supervisors. The Chancery Clerk can describe how your county runs it. The normal filing cutoff is the first Monday in August.

Supervisors review the assessor's values, listen to taxpayer objections and adopt the rolls. Keep these points in mind while you prepare:

  • Only the value is up for debate. The county, city and school district set millage separately.
  • If the assessor used the wrong square footage, a refund for earlier years may be possible. Ask the Chancery Clerk.
  • When a bill climbs, the cause is value, rate, or both.

Thinking of selling soon? Ask the Chancery Clerk and Tax Collector how they treat an appeal that is still open, and let the title company confirm the balance.

sections.h2: When the tax is not paid
sections.html:
Paying late adds penalties and interest. Parcels that remain delinquent are put up at the county tax auction. Depending on the county, that auction is the first Monday in April or the last Monday in August.

The Chancery Clerk runs each year's sale, keeps the paperwork, and can quote the cost of redeeming a parcel that was sold. A parcel with no buyer goes to the State of Mississippi, with the Secretary of State as manager. Their phone number is 1-866-835-2637.

Questions about a sale go to the tax collector in the county where the property is located. If you owe delinquent tax, ask for the balance and any redemption figure well before closing.

sections.h2: Paying the bill and what to bring
sections.html:
Before you pay or dispute anything, collect the paper you will need. The tax bill itself shows the parcel and the millage that applies. The legal description comes from the Chancery Clerk. Receipts for earlier years help if a title company asks for proof that nothing is open.

Then work through the offices in order. Call the Tax Assessor about value and class. Call the Tax Collector about the balance and how to pay. Call the Chancery Clerk about appeals, land records and tax sale questions. Keep a short note of who you spoke with and when, since closing agents often ask for it, and if you decide to sell to a cash buyer the same notes make the process faster.

Sellers most often hit one of three snags: a prior-year bill still open, a homestead exemption that lapsed or was never filed, or a class change on a house that is empty. An heir whose inherited house is no longer owner-occupied should ask the Tax Assessor whether the ratio moves from 10% to 15% of true value.

  • Get the tax bill and legal description from the Tax Collector and Chancery Clerk.
  • Ask if homestead was claimed and whether a disallowance is pending.
  • Have the title company check the current-year bill and any tax sale history.
  • If the estate is in probate, our Mississippi probate guide explains who can sign.

We buy Mississippi houses as-is, including ones with tax due or deferred repairs, and we reply with a written offer. We make no promise on price in this guide.

faqs.q: What is the Mississippi property tax rate?
faqs.a: No single statewide rate exists. Each property owes a county millage and a school district millage, plus a city or special district rate where one applies. The tax is true value times the assessment ratio times total millage, and Class I homes are assessed at 10% of true value.

faqs.q: When are Mississippi property taxes due?
faqs.a: By February 1 for property assessed the previous year. If that date is a weekend or legal holiday, the following Monday is the last penalty-free day.

faqs.q: Can I appeal my Mississippi property assessment?
faqs.a: Yes. Ask the Chancery Clerk to set a hearing with the county Board of Supervisors. File by the first Monday in August, ahead of the due date.

faqs.q: When must I apply for homestead exemption in Mississippi?
faqs.a: Between January 1 and April 1, at the county Tax Assessor. An application after April 1 misses that assessment year.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house in Mississippi with property tax due?
faqs.a: Yes. A cash buyer can take the house as-is, and the title company confirms the amount owed before closing. Taxes left delinquent can lead to the county tax auction, so check the balance and any redemption figure first.
